newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Prosecutors charge man behind Ceausescu fall.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors charge man behind Ceausescu fall.

text.p: The general who persuaded Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceausescu to flee Bucharest in 1989 was charged on Thursday with misuse of public funds costing the defence ministry the equivalent of $8 million.

Military prosecutors filed the charges against Victor Atanasie Stanculescu, defence, economy and industry minister in Romania's first post-communist government, in connection with the purchase of communications equipment.
The 62-page indictment was submitted to the Supreme Court's military section. A date for the trial has yet to be set.
"Stanculescu, as defence minister, approved in 1990 a procurement operation which caused damages to the defence budget equivalent to $8,053,147," said the indictment, made available to Reuters.
Stanculescu, 69, charged with four army officers and three civilians, faces up to five years in jail if convicted. He was not immediatly available to comment.
The trial will be the latest in a series launched after last November's elections when President Emil Constantinescu and a centrist government ended seven years of rule by ex-communists.

The president has pledged to unmask and punish officials guilty of corruption since the 1989 fall of communism. An anti-corruption commission has already recovered the equivalent of $63 million in embezzled funds.

Stanculescu, a retired army general turned businessman, held key jobs under Ceausescu, including more than 10 years as head of army procurement, a job he held when the revolution erupted in December 1989.
At the start of unrest in the western city of Timisoara, Stanculescu put his leg in a plaster cast to avoid carrying out Ceausescu's orders to have the army turn their guns on demonstrators.
Days later he persuaded Ceausescu and his wife Elena to flee Bucharest by helicopter and attended their summary trial before a firing squad executed the couple on Christmas Day.
